{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01DWTEYhVvi47Y9bUsK11Mpq","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Architecture and Build Plan Template\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections below in this order. Headings may be renamed slightly to suit the domain, but keep the order and intent. For small systems, a section may be a single sentence. If a section does not apply, keep its heading and give a one-line reason. Prefer tables where the notes suggest them.\n4\t\n5\t---\n6\t\n7\t## 1. Summary\n8\t\n9\tFive to ten sentences or a tight bullet list covering:\n10\t\n11\t- What is being built and for whom.\n12\t- The overall shape of the architecture in one or two sentences.\n13\t- The three to five most important decisions.\n14\t- What the first milestone delivers.\n15\t- The top risks.\n16\t\n17\tSomeone who reads only this section should know what is about to happen and why.\n18\t\n19\t## 2. Context and Goals\n20\t\n21\t- **Problem:** what is painful or missing today, and for whom.\n22\t- **Goals:** the outcomes the system must achieve, in measurable terms where possible.\n23\t- **Non-goals:** things deliberately left out of scope, so nobody assumes they are coming.\n24\t- **Success measures:** how you will know it worked after launch, such as adoption, latency, cost, accuracy, or time saved.\n25\t\n26\t## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n27\t\n28\t- **Ranked quality attributes:** a table with the columns *attribute*, *measurable target*, and *why it matters*, in priority order. Mark targets you inferred as assumptions.\n29\t- **Key functional requirements:** the capabilities that shape the structure. This is not a full backlog.\n30\t- **Constraints:** existing stack, hosting, team size and skills, deadline, budget, compliance, data residency, and mandated vendors.\n31\t- **Hard parts:** the few areas that are new, uncertain, dependent on outside parties, or costly to get wrong, each with one sentence on why.\n32\t\n33\t## 4. Current State\n34\t\n35\tWhat exists today that this work touches: relevant code, services, data stores, infrastructure, and processes. Cite specific files, modules, or systems where you inspected them. Note conventions the plan will follow. For entirely new builds, state what organisational or platform context applies.\n36\t\n37\t## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n38\t\n39\t- **Assumptions:** a table with the columns *assumption*, *impact if wrong*, and *how and when it will be validated*.\n40\t- **Open questions:** each with the owner or person who can answer it, the default you will use if no answer arrives, and the date or milestone by which it must be resolved.\n41\t\n42\t## 6. Architecture Overview\n43\t\n44\t- A text-based diagram (Mermaid or ASCII) showing components, data stores, external systems, and trust boundaries.\n45\t- A short narrative of how the parts fit together.\n46\t- A **component table** with the columns *component*, *responsibility*, *owns which data*, *exposes which interfaces*, *technology*, and *key dependencies*.\n47\t\n48\t## 7. Component Details\n49\t\n50\tFor each significant component:\n51\t\n52\t- Its responsibility and its boundaries, meaning what it explicitly does not do.\n53\t- Its interfaces: whether they are synchronous or asynchronous, the contract format, how they are versioned, and the expected load.\n54\t- Its internal structure, where that matters.\n55\t- How it fails and how it recovers.\n56\t- How it scales, if scale is a driver.\n57\t\n58\tRoutine components can be covered in a line or two.\n59\t\n60\t## 8. Data Design\n61\t\n62\t- The main entities and how they relate to each other.\n63\t- The system of record for each entity, and which component writes to it.\n64\t- Consistency requirements and where transactions are needed.\n65\t- Access patterns and the indexing or partitioning they imply.\n66\t- Retention, deletion, backup, and restore targets.\n67\t- Data classification, covering sensitive fields and how they are protected.\n68\t- How schemas will evolve and how migrations will be done.\n69\t\n70\t## 9. Key Flows\n71\t\n72\tWalk through the two to four most important scenarios step by step, from trigger to outcome. Use sequence diagrams or numbered steps. Include at least one failure path, such as a timeout, retry, duplicate, partial failure, or dependency outage, and show how the system behaves.\n73\t\n74\t## 10. Key Decisions\n75\t\n76\tOne entry per significant decision, optionally as a table:\n77\t\n78\t- **Decision:** what was decided.\n79\t- **Options considered:** at least two realistic ones.\n80\t- **Rationale:** why this option, measured against the ranked drivers.\n81\t- **Reversibility:** whether it is hard or easy to undo.\n82\t- **Revisit if:** the evidence or condition that would reopen the decision.\n83\t\n84\t## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n85\t\n86\tA short subsection for each. Name the concrete mechanism and the milestone in which it is built.\n87\t\n88\t- **Security:** identity, authorisation model, secrets, encryption, input validation, the main threats and their mitigations.\n89\t- **Reliability:** availability and recovery targets, redundancy, timeouts, retries, idempotency, backpressure.\n90\t- **Observability:** logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, alerts tied to user-facing symptoms.\n91\t- **Performance and capacity:** expected load, the bottlenecks you expect, and how they will be load-tested.\n92\t- **Cost:** estimated run cost, the main cost drivers, and the controls on spend.\n93\t- **Operations:** who owns the system, runbooks, on-call expectations, and how support works.\n94\t- **AI-specific concerns, where relevant:** evaluation approach, guardrails, cost and latency budgets, human approval points, and the fallback when the model fails.\n95\t\n96\t## 12. Build Sequence\n97\t\n98\tA milestone table or list. For each milestone:\n99\t\n100\t- **Goal:** the risk it clears or the value it delivers.\n101\t- **Scope:** what is included and what is explicitly excluded.\n102\t- **Deliverables:** the concrete artefacts, features, or environments it produces.\n103\t- **Exit criteria:** checkable conditions that mark it complete.\n104\t- **Dependencies:** what must be finished first, and what can run in parallel.\n105\t- **Rough size:** a range, with the team assumption behind it.\n106\t\n107\tThe first milestone must contain a thin end-to-end slice and the spikes for the highest-risk unknowns. Mark the critical path.\n108\t\n109\t## 13. First Milestone Task Breakdown\n110\t\n111\tA list of concrete tasks. Each one has a verb and a deliverable, its location (module, directory, service, or repository), and a \"done when\" condition. Note the order and which tasks can run in parallel. Spikes include the question being answered, a time box, and the result that would change the plan.\n112\t\n113\t## 14. Testing and Validation Strategy\n114\t\n115\t- Which kinds of tests cover which risks: unit, contract, integration, end-to-end, load, security, and evaluation sets for AI components.\n116\t- The test environments and test data needed.\n117\t- What runs in CI and what blocks a release.\n118\t- How the measurable targets in Section 3 will actually be verified.\n119\t\n120\t## 15. Rollout, Migration, and Rollback\n121\t\n122\t- How the system reaches users: feature flags, staged or percentage rollout, beta groups.\n123\t- For changes to existing systems: how old and new run side by side, the steps for migrating data, and the switchover criteria.\n124\t- The rollback procedure for each risky step, and the point after which rolling back is no longer possible.\n125\t\n126\t## 16. Risks and Mitigations\n127\t\n128\tA table with the columns *risk*, *likelihood*, *impact*, *mitigation*, *early warning sign*, and *owner*. Include technical, delivery, dependency, and organisational risks.\n129\t\n130\t## 17. Deferred Work and Future Evolution\n131\t\n132\t- Items deliberately postponed, and what would trigger building each one.\n133\t- Ways the architecture is expected to evolve, and the extension points that support it.\n134\t- Known shortcuts or technical debt taken on purpose, with a plan to pay each one back.\n135\t\n136\t## 18. Next Steps\n137\t\n138\tThree to seven actions someone can take immediately. These include answering the open questions that block progress and starting the first tasks. Name the specific files, commands, or people where possible.\n139\t"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"f8f633d2-7e34-4ac5-bbc7-b442e8a33289","uuid":"341c77fe-093d-4aa9-9903-b8acc46090bf","timestamp":"2026-10-03T02:18:59.110Z","tool_use_result":{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\\Users\\nrvhari\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\dfa-eval\\2026-10-03-outcomes-webhook-ledger\\plugins\\p2ab33809\\skills\\architecture-planner\\reference\\document-template.md","content":"# Architecture and Build Plan Template\n\nUse the sections below in this order. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_015eLCU7iBTFxGFbUxrkndCH","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Planning Guidance and Checklists\n2\t\n3\tUse the sections that are relevant. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n4\t\n5\t## 1. Discovery questions\n6\t\n7\tChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n8\t\n9\t- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n10\t- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n11\t- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n12\t- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n13\t- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n14\t- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n15\t- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n16\t- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n17\t- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n18\t- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n19\t\n20\t## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n21\t\n22\t| Attribute | Express it as |\n23\t|---|---|\n24\t| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n25\t| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n26\t| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n27\t| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n28\t| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n29\t| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n30\t| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n31\t| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n32\t| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n33\t\n34\tIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n35\t\n36\t## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n37\t\n38\t- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n39\t- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n40\t- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n41\t- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n42\t- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n43\t- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n44\t- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n45\t\n46\t## 4. Data checklist\n47\t\n48\t- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n49\t- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n50\t- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n51\t- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n52\t- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n53\t- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n54\t- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n55\t- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n56\t\n57\t## 5. Choosing technology\n58\t\n59\t- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n60\t- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n61\t- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n62\t- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n63\t- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n64\t- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n65\t\n66\t## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n67\t\n68\t- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n69\t- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n70\t- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n71\t- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n72\t- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n73\t- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n74\t- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n75\t\n76\t## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n77\t\n78\tA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n79\t\n80\t- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n81\t- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Map provider groups to the `admin` and `member` roles. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n84\t\n85\tKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n86\t\n87\t## 8. Security checklist\n88\t\n89\t- Identity: how users and services authenticate, and where sessions or tokens are checked.\n90\t- Authorisation: the permission model (roles, attributes, or ownership), enforced on the server side for every request.\n91\t- Secrets: stored in a secret manager, never in code or images, and rotatable.\n92\t- Encryption in transit everywhere. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n93\t- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. Parameterised queries.\n94\t- Least privilege for service accounts, infrastructure roles, and AI tool permissions.\n95\t- Dependency and image scanning in CI. A plan for applying patches.\n96\t- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n97\t- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n98\t\n99\t## 9. Reliability and operations checklist\n100\t\n101\t- A timeout on every network call, retries with backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, and circuit breaking for fragile dependencies.\n102\t- Idempotency keys for operations that may be retried or delivered twice.\n103\t- Backpressure and queue limits, plus dead-letter handling and a process for reprocessing failed messages.\n104\t- Health checks that reflect whether the system can actually serve requests, not just whether the process is running.\n105\t- Alerts based on symptoms users would notice, each linked to a runbook.\n106\t- Structured logs with correlation IDs that can be followed across components.\n107\t- Deployments that are automated, repeatable, and reversible, with an explicit rollback procedure.\n108\t- A capacity plan and a load test at or above the expected peak before launch.\n109\t- Clear ownership: who is on call, how incidents are handled, and who approves changes.\n110\t\n111\t## 10. AI and agentic systems checklist\n112\t\n113\t- **Evaluation first:** a representative, versioned evaluation set with clear pass criteria, run automatically whenever prompts, models, or tools change. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n114\t- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. Add autonomy, planning loops, or multiple agents only when evaluations show they are needed.\n115\t- **Model choice:** weigh quality, latency, cost, context size, and data-handling terms. Keep model access behind an interface so models can be swapped.\n116\t- **Prompts and configuration:** under version control, reviewed, and tied to evaluation results.\n117\t- **Tools:** narrow, well-described interfaces with validated arguments, least-privilege credentials, and dry-run or confirmation modes for actions that can't be undone.\n118\t- **Limits:** a maximum number of steps, a token and spend budget per task, wall-clock timeouts, and loop detection.\n119\t- **Human oversight:** approval points before irreversible or high-impact actions, and a clear way to hand off to a person.\n120\t- **Untrusted input:** treat retrieved documents, tool outputs, and user content as possible injected instructions. These are thinking aids, not forms to fill in. Skip items that clearly don't apply, and go deeper wherever the hard parts are.\n\n## 1. Discovery questions\n\nChoose the questions whose answers would change the design. If you can't ask, choose a default and record it as an assumption.\n\n- Who are the users, how many are there, and where are they? Is the system internal, B2B, or consumer-facing?\n- What is the busiest realistic hour? How much data arrives each day, and how much is kept in total?\n- What is the cost of downtime, of losing data, and of returning a wrong answer? These answers set the reliability and correctness targets.\n- Is the system single-tenant or multi-tenant? Do tenants need their data isolated?\n- What data is regulated or sensitive (personal, health, payment, or confidential data)? Are there residency rules?\n- What must the system integrate with? Are those systems reliable and documented, and who owns them?\n- What stack, cloud, and tooling are already in use or required by the organisation?\n- How many engineers are there, what are their strengths, and how much operational work can they take on?\n- Is there a fixed date? What is the smallest release that would still be valuable?\n- What has been tried before, and why didn't it work?\n\n## 2. Making quality attributes measurable\n\n| Attribute | Express it as |\n|---|---|\n| Latency | Percentile at a given load, e.g. p95 < 250 ms at 100 rps |\n| Availability | Percentage over a window plus maintenance policy, e.g. 99.9% monthly |\n| Recovery | Maximum time to restore and maximum acceptable data loss |\n| Throughput | Sustained and peak rates, with expected growth |\n| Correctness | Error budget or accuracy threshold on a defined evaluation set |\n| Cost | Monthly run cost ceiling, or cost per user, request, or task |\n| Security | Named threats that must be mitigated, plus compliance obligations |\n| Evolvability | The changes that must be cheap, e.g. \"add a new payment provider in under a week\" |\n| Time to market | The date by which a specific capability must be live |\n\nIf a target was invented, label it as an assumption and say how it will be confirmed.\n\n## 3. Decomposition heuristics\n\n- Draw boundaries around business capabilities and the data they own, not around technical layers.\n- Things that change together belong together. Things that change for different reasons should be separated.\n- Each piece of data should have exactly one writer. Shared writable tables between components are a warning sign.\n- Split into separately deployed services only when there is a clear reason: different scaling needs, separate team ownership, different security zones, or different release cadences. Otherwise keep modules inside one deployable unit, with boundaries enforced in code.\n- Keep synchronous call chains short. Use asynchronous messaging where work can be delayed or must survive outages. Accept that this brings eventual consistency and harder debugging.\n- Wrap each external dependency behind your own interface, so it can be replaced, faked in tests, and protected from failures.\n- Check every boundary with one question: can this component be tested and changed without coordinating with the others?\n\n## 4. Data checklist\n\n- Which component is the system of record for each entity?\n- Which operations need atomicity, and do they cross component boundaries? If so, plan for idempotent steps, compensating actions, or an outbox pattern for publishing events reliably.\n- What are the main read and write paths, and which indexes, caches, or read models do they require?\n- How will the schema change without downtime? Use additive changes first, a backfill, a switch of reads, and only then removal of the old structure.\n- What are the retention and deletion obligations, including user deletion requests and legal holds?\n- What are the backup frequency, the restore targets, and the date of the last tested restore?\n- Which fields are sensitive, and are they encrypted, masked in logs, and access-controlled?\n- How will production-like test data be produced without copying sensitive data?\n\n## 5. Choosing technology\n\n- Start with what the team already knows and what the organisation already runs.\n- Prefer managed services when the team is small or operational appetite is low.\n- Before adopting something new, name the driver it satisfies that the existing option can't, and include the cost of learning it and running it.\n- Check for limits that could stop you later: licensing, quotas, regional availability, maximum sizes, rate limits, and whether you can get your data out.\n- Note any decision that ties you deeply to one vendor, and record what leaving would cost.\n- Avoid adopting several new technologies in the same milestone, because it makes failures hard to diagnose.\n\n## 6. Sequencing heuristics\n\n- **First slice:** pick the most representative user scenario and build only enough of each layer to complete it, deployed through the real pipeline to a real environment. Use hard-coded or stubbed pieces freely, but list them.\n- **Spikes:** each one has a question, a time box (typically one to five days), something you can examine at the end, and a result that would change the plan. Schedule them before work that depends on their answers.\n- **Critical path:** find the longest chain of dependent work and start it first. Look for long-lead items such as vendor access, security reviews, procurement, data-sharing agreements, and quota increases. Request them on day one.\n- **Parallel work:** once the interfaces are agreed, independent components can be built at the same time against contracts or fakes.\n- **Milestone size:** aim for milestones that take a few weeks at most and end in something you can demonstrate. Long milestones hide risk.\n- **Hardening:** don't leave all security, performance, and operational work to a final phase. Build each in when its component is built, then verify it before launch.\n- **Order of migrations:** build the new path, run it in parallel or shadow mode, compare results, move traffic over gradually, and only then retire the old path.\n\n## 7. Writing actionable tasks\n\nA good task has a verb, a specific deliverable, a location, and a \"done when\" condition that someone else can check.\n\n- Weak: \"Implement auth.\"\n- Strong: \"Add OIDC login with the organisation's identity provider in `services/api/auth/`. Done when an integration test logs in a test user from each group and receives the correct permissions.\"\n- Weak: \"Set up monitoring.\"\n- Strong: \"Emit request count, error rate, and p95 latency per endpoint from the API to the existing metrics stack. Add an alert when the error rate exceeds 2% for 5 minutes. Done when a deliberately injected failure in staging triggers the alert.\"\n\nKeep each task to a few days of work at most. Split anything larger.\n\n## 8. Security checklist\n\n- Identity: how users and services authenticate, and where sessions or tokens are checked.\n- Authorisation: the permission model (roles, attributes, or ownership), enforced on the server side for every request.\n- Secrets: stored in a secret manager, never in code or images, and rotatable.\n- Encryption in transit everywhere. Encryption at rest for sensitive stores.\n- Input validation and output encoding at every trust boundary. Parameterised queries.\n- Least privilege for service accounts, infrastructure roles, and AI tool permissions.\n- Dependency and image scanning in CI. A plan for applying patches.\n- Audit logs for security-relevant actions, protected from tampering.\n- The three to five most likely threats for this specific system, each paired with a mitigation.\n\n## 9. Reliability and operations checklist\n\n- A timeout on every network call, retries with backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, and circuit breaking for fragile dependencies.\n- Idempotency keys for operations that may be retried or delivered twice.\n- Backpressure and queue limits, plus dead-letter handling and a process for reprocessing failed messages.\n- Health checks that reflect whether the system can actually serve requests, not just whether the process is running.\n- Alerts based on symptoms users would notice, each linked to a runbook.\n- Structured logs with correlation IDs that can be followed across components.\n- Deployments that are automated, repeatable, and reversible, with an explicit rollback procedure.\n- A capacity plan and a load test at or above the expected peak before launch.\n- Clear ownership: who is on call, how incidents are handled, and who approves changes.\n\n## 10. Include adversarial and edge cases.\n- **Simplest design that passes:** start with one model call or a fixed pipeline. State split so a single change can only affect a limited area.\n- Identity, account or project layout, and network design planned first, because they are the hardest to change later.\n- Changes promoted from development to staging to production, with automated checks at each stage.\n- Quotas, limits, and regional capacity checked early.\n- Cost tagging, budgets, and alerts.\n- Backup, disaster recovery, and failover procedures, each tested.\n\n## 12. Old systems that are never retired double the operational cost.\n\n## 13. Common failure modes to check against\n\n- The architecture serves a scale or level of flexibility nobody asked for.\n- Weeks of foundation work with nothing demonstrable at the end.\n- Integration and deployment attempted for the first time near the deadline.\n- Several components writing to the same data, so ownership is unclear.\n- No plan for schema changes, backfills, or rollback.\n- AI behaviour assumed rather than measured.\n- Long-lead dependencies discovered late.\n- Estimates given as single numbers with no stated assumptions.\n- Decisions presented as lists of options with no recommendation.\n","numLines":157,"startLine":1,"totalLines":157}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_u2uj34vi2voh35hflpl5yt3umk3txlta6gvwymht4mibginyfrsa","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# Ledger: Architecture and Build Plan\n\n> **Read this first: what I could and couldn't see.** The workspace has only a `README.md`. It says the directory is intentionally empty and does **not** document `ledgerkit` or `MemoryStore`, even though the brief points there. I couldn't see which operations the store supports. That matters more than anything else in this plan, because how we survive `StoreError` partway through a request depends on whether the store has conditional writes or transactions. Below I design against a small set of store operations I'm assuming exist (§5, A1). I also give the fallback if they don't. Checking this is the first task (T1).\n\n---\n\n## 1. Summary\n\n- **What:** Ledger is a stdlib-only Python library, `LedgerService`. It turns signed PayCo webhooks into per-account balances and entry lists that Finance can reconcile against PayCo's monthly statement, to the minor unit. It replaces the nightly CSV-to-spreadsheet script and the manual balance fixes.\n- **Shape:** One synchronous library called by a thin HTTP adapter. Internally it has a functional core and a thin I/O layer: pure modules for signature checking, parsing and balance rules, plus one repository module that talks to the store. There is no queue and no second service. PayCo's 72-hour retries act as our retry queue.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. **One atomic write moves money.** Each account's state (balance, entries, payment index, parked refunds, IDs of applied events) lives in one account document. It changes only through a single compare-and-set write, which is the commit point. A `StoreError` at any point leaves either \"nothing happened\" or \"everything happened\", and PayCo's redelivery finishes the job.\n  2. **Return 2xx only after the effect is durable.** A duplicate is recognised from the account document (the event was applied), not from a separate \"seen\" flag. A crash between \"seen\" and \"applied\" therefore can't lose money.\n  3. **Write-once event record** keyed by event `id`, holding the SHA-256 of the raw body. If the same `id` arrives with a different body, we return 409, raise an alert, and leave the account untouched. The record also covers unknown event types and stores their raw body, so we can replay them once we support disputes and payouts.\n  4. **A refund that arrives before its payment is parked** (202) inside the account document. It is settled in the same atomic write that later applies the payment. We don't reject it and hope PayCo's retries outlast the gap.\n  5. **Strict input handling:** we verify the HMAC over the raw bytes before parsing, allow ±300 s on the timestamp, compare in constant time, and parse JSON strictly (duplicate keys, floats, booleans and NaN are rejected as amounts).\n- **First milestone:** two short spikes (store semantics, and how PayCo signs retries) and the payment path end to end. It includes signature checks, deduplication, the different-body check, unknown types, and a test that injects a fault at every write and shows redelivery always ends in the same state as a fault-free run.\n- **Top risks:** the store has no conditional write (A1); PayCo retries reuse the original `t`, so retries more than 5 minutes later fail the timestamp check (A2); refunds of payments made before cutover arrive with no matching payment (§15).\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem:** Balances are rebuilt nightly from a CSV and fixed by hand. They are up to 24 hours stale, errors are possible, and support staff spend time on it.\n- **Goals:**\n  - Every validly signed PayCo payment and refund ends up applied **exactly once**, or is visibly parked or rejected. Nothing is silently lost or doubled.\n  - A balance reflects a payment within about 60 s of PayCo sending it, in normal operation (assumption).\n  - Survive `StoreError`, duplicate delivery, out-of-order delivery and concurrent delivery without manual repair.\n- **Non-goals:** debiting customer spend (not in the interface; see Q2), partial refunds, disputes, payouts and other event types (recorded but not applied), multi-currency accounts, the HTTP server, deployment and monitoring stack (covered here as guidance only), and secret rotation with two secrets live at once (deferred, §17).\n- **Success measures:** zero unexplained differences in the first two monthly reconciliations after cutover; zero manual balance edits; nightly script retired; no 409 that isn't explained.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes**\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it matters |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Financial correctness | 0 unexplained differences per account per monthly reconciliation. In a seeded simulation of 10k events with shuffled order, duplicates and injected faults, final state equals the oracle (an independent calculation of the expected result) | Finance needs an exact match; a wrong balance is real money |\n| 2 | Authenticity and integrity | 0 money movements from unsigned, stale (>300 s) or different-body deliveries; every different-body case alerts within 5 min | Webhook endpoints are public; the brief makes different-body reuse an incident |\n| 3 | Recovery from partial failure | For every write position *k* in a request, with a `StoreError` before or after it commits, redelivery ends in the same state as a fault-free run | The store fails partway through requests |\n| 4 | Evolvability | Adding a new event type (e.g. `charge.dispute.*`) in ≤1 week with no change to stored data shape, plus replay of events already received | PayCo adds types; \"we will add them later\" |\n| 5 | Operability and simplicity | One deployable unit; ≤5 alert types; on-call needs no store access for routine cases *(assumption)* | Small team, small volume |\n| — | Latency and throughput | p99 handling < 1 s at 10 req/s *(assumption; about 100× today's volume)* | Not a driver at a few thousand events a day. Recorded so nobody over-builds |\n\n**Key functional requirements:** verify the signature and timestamp; credit `payment.succeeded`; debit `refund.succeeded` once per payment, with the amount equal to the payment; the account currency is fixed by its first payment; a different body under the same `id` is rejected; unknown types are accepted and not applied; `balance` and `entries` match the interface in the brief.\n\n**Constraints:** Python, standard library only; the store is a `ledgerkit` MemoryStore client (API unknown to me); the interface signatures are fixed; HTTP, deployment and monitoring live outside this codebase.\n\n**Hard parts**\n\n1. **Atomicity against a store that fails partway through.** If we mark an event \"processed\" before the money moves, a crash loses money for good, because the redelivery looks like a duplicate.\n2. **Out-of-order and concurrent pairs.** A refund that arrives before its payment, or both arriving at the same moment, can leave a refund parked forever unless both are serialised on one record.\n3. **Cutover.** Refunds of payments made before go-live, and opening balances. Easy to miss, and expensive if missed.\n4. **PayCo delivery details we haven't verified:** whether retries get a fresh `t`, and whether redelivered bodies are byte-identical.\n\n## 4. Current State\n\n- **Code:** none. `README.md` is the only file and says so. `ledgerkit` is not in the workspace, so its API, version and the exact behaviour of `StoreError` are unknown.\n- **Process:** a nightly script copies PayCo's CSV export into a spreadsheet, and support staff fix balances by hand. This is the system Ledger replaces, and the source of opening balances (§15).\n- **Conventions I'll set, since none exist:** package `ledger/`, tests in `tests/` run with `python -m unittest`, no third-party packages apart from `ledgerkit`, Python ≥3.11 *(assumption A8)*.\n\n## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n\n**Assumptions**\n\n| # | Assumption | Impact if wrong | How and when validated |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| A1 | The store offers single-key get, put-if-absent, and compare-and-set (or a transaction). A single write is never left half-applied. | Without a conditional write: fall back to one writer process with per-account locks (D1b). With half-applied writes: no client-side design is safe, so escalate to the DB owner. | T1 spike, day 1 |\n| A2 | Each PayCo retry is signed again with a fresh `t`. | Retries more than 300 s later always fail, so our 503s never recover. We'd need to retry inside the request and escalate to PayCo. | T2 sandbox spike, M1 |\n| A3 | Redeliveries are byte-identical (the brief says \"same body\"). | False 409s on events already applied. No money effect, but alert noise. | T2; incident logs also record whether canonical JSON matched |\n| A4 | At most one `refund.succeeded` per `payment_id` (refunds are always full). Refund `account_id` equals the payment's. | Second refund rejected (422); mismatched account leaves the refund parked and alerting | Ask PayCo; watch anomaly alerts |\n| A5 | One `payment.succeeded` per `payment_id`. | Treated as an anomaly (422) rather than a double credit | T2 fixtures; PayCo docs |\n| A6 | Spending is debited somewhere else, or later. Ledger's balance = payments − refunds. | Interface and data model would grow a debit path (Q2) | Ask the product owner before M3 |\n| A7 | The HTTP layer passes the raw request bytes unchanged, case-varying headers as a `dict[str,str]`, and caps body size. | Signatures fail, or we have a DoS hole | M3 adapter contract test |\n| A8 | Python ≥3.11. | Minor syntax changes only | T0 |\n| A9 | Event records and entries are kept indefinitely (financial records). About 1 MB/day of raw bodies. | Storage cost, but small | Ask Finance about retention policy, M3 |\n\n**Open questions**\n\n| Question | Owner | Default if no answer | Needed by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Q1 What is the MemoryStore / production client API? Does production use the same API? | Whoever owns `ledgerkit` | A1 | T1, day 1 (blocking) |\n| Q2 How does spending relate to this balance, and what opening balance does each account start with at cutover? | Product + Finance | Ledger tracks PayCo movements only; history is imported from the PayCo export | Start of M3 |\n| Q3 Can we have PayCo sandbox access? What is PayCo's delivery timeout? Can it resend a specific event by hand? | Whoever holds the PayCo account | Assume a 10 s timeout and no manual resend | Request day 1; needed for T2 |\n| Q4 For a signed event that breaks a rule (currency mismatch, double refund): reply 422 so PayCo keeps retrying, or 2xx and quarantine? | Finance + on-call owner | 422 **and** a durable anomaly record | End of M2 |\n| Q5 Should `entries()` be ordered by when we applied each entry (default) or by PayCo `created`? | Finance | Order we applied them; `created` included in each entry | End of M1 |\n\n## 6. Architecture Overview\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n  PayCo[(PayCo)] -- \"HTTPS POST + PayCo-Signature\" --> HTTP\n  subgraph Trust boundary: our network\n    HTTP[\"HTTP adapter (outside this codebase)<br/>raw bytes, size cap, TLS\"] --> SVC\n    subgraph ledger package\n      SVC[LedgerService<br/>service.py] --> SIG[signature.py]\n      SVC --> EVT[events.py]\n      SVC --> RUL[rules.py<br/>pure state transitions]\n      SVC --> REPO[repository.py]\n    end\n    REPO --> DB[(ledgerkit store<br/>event:* / account:* / anomaly:*)]\n    Product[Product / support tools] -- \"balance(), entries()\" --> SVC\n    Tools[tools/reconcile.py<br/>tools/import_history.py] --> REPO\n  end\n  CSV[(PayCo monthly statement / CSV export)] --> Tools\n```\n\n**How it fits together:** `handle()` checks the signature and timestamp against the raw bytes. It then parses strictly and writes or reads the write-once event record, which is where a different body under the same `id` is caught. Finally it runs a compare-and-set loop on the account document. Inside that loop, the pure `rules.apply(state, event)` decides the outcome. Reads (`balance`, `entries`) load the account document. Only `repository.py` touches the store.\n\n| Component | Responsibility | Owns data | Interfaces | Technology | Dependencies |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `LedgerService` (`service.py`) | Orchestrate; map outcomes to status codes; read API | none | `handle`, `balance`, `entries` (sync, in process) | stdlib | all below, `clock` |\n| Signature verifier (`signature.py`) | Parse header, check HMAC and ±300 s | none | `verify(raw, headers, secret, now) -> ok \\| Reason` | `hmac`, `hashlib`, `re` | — |\n| Event parser (`events.py`) | Strict JSON and per-type validation into dataclasses | none | `parse_envelope(raw)`, `validate(envelope) -> Payment \\| Refund` | `json`, `dataclasses` | — |\n| Ledger rules (`rules.py`) | Pure account state change and outcome | none (pure) | `apply(state, event, now) -> (new_state \\| None, Outcome)` | stdlib | — |\n| Repository (`repository.py`) | The only code that calls the store; compare-and-set loop | `event:*`, `account:*`, `anomaly:*` | `put_event_if_absent`, `update_account(id, fn)`, `load_account`, `put_anomaly` | `ledgerkit` | store |\n| Tools (M3) | Reconciliation and history import | writes only through the repository | CLI | stdlib `csv` | PayCo export |\n\n## 7. Component Details\n\n**Signature verifier.**\n- Look up the header case-insensitively. If two keys differ only in case (e.g. `PayCo-Signature` and `payco-signature`), return 400.\n- Split the header value on `,`, then each part on the first `=`. Require exactly one `t` matching `[0-9]{1,12}`. Don't use bare `int()`, which accepts `+1`, `1_000` and Unicode digits.\n- Accept one or more `v1` values, each matching `[0-9a-f]{64}`. Checking the format first also avoids a `TypeError` that `compare_digest` raises on non-ASCII strings.\n- Expected value: `HMAC-SHA256(secret, t_str.encode() + b\".\" + raw_body)`, using the **original `t` string**. Compare with `hmac.compare_digest` against each `v1`.\n- Check the signature first, then `abs(clock.now() - int(t)) > 300` → reject. This is inclusive at exactly 300 s.\n- Out of scope: JSON, and replay deduplication. A replay inside the 300 s window is harmless because of event-`id` idempotency.\n\n**Event parser.**\n- `json.loads` with an `object_pairs_hook` that rejects duplicate keys, and a `parse_constant` that rejects NaN and Infinity. The top level must be an object, and `id` a non-empty string.\n- For known types, check `data`: `account_id` and `payment_id` non-empty strings; `amount` with `type(x) is int` (Python treats `True` as an `int`) and `> 0`; `currency` matching `[A-Z]{3}`; `created` an int.\n- Unknown types get only the envelope check.\n\n**Ledger rules (pure).** This is where the money logic lives, so it gets the most tests.\n- `payment.succeeded`:\n  - Event already in `applied_event_ids` → DUPLICATE.\n  - `payment_id` already in `payments` from a different event → REJECT `duplicate_payment`.\n  - Currency set and different from the event's → REJECT `currency_mismatch`.\n  - Otherwise: set the currency if unset, add the entry `+amount`, record the payment.\n  - If `pending_refunds[payment_id]` exists and matches on amount and currency, settle it in the same state: add a `-amount` entry and mark the payment refunded. If it doesn't match, keep it parked with `mismatch` set so the parked-refund alert fires.\n- `refund.succeeded`:\n  - Already applied, or already parked with the same event → DUPLICATE or PENDING.\n  - Payment unknown → PARK, keyed by `payment_id`. If a different event is already parked for that payment → REJECT `double_refund`.\n  - Payment already refunded → REJECT `double_refund`.\n  - Amount or currency differs from the payment → REJECT `refund_mismatch`.\n  - Otherwise add the entry `-amount`.\n- A refund never fails for lack of balance. Negative balances are allowed and recorded, because refusing a refund would break reconciliation.\n\n**Repository.**\n- `put_event_if_absent(id, record)` returns the record already stored, if any.\n- `update_account(id, fn)`: load (document and version) → `fn` → compare-and-set. On a version conflict, retry up to 5 times, then raise `Contention`, which becomes 503.\n- `StoreError` is never caught here. It goes up to the service.\n\n**`handle()` in outline**\n\n```\nheaders → signature.verify            → 400/401 on failure\nraw → events.parse_envelope           → 400 on failure\ndigest = sha256(raw)\ntry:\n  rec = repo.put_event_if_absent(id, {digest, type, raw_body, first_seen_at})\n  if rec.digest != digest: log INCIDENT (incl. canonical-JSON-equal flag) → 409\n  if type not in HANDLERS: → 200 ignored\n  ev = events.validate(envelope)      → on error: repo.put_anomaly(id, …) → 422\n  outcome = repo.update_account(ev.account_id, λs: rules.apply(s, ev, now))\n  REJECTED → repo.put_anomaly(id, …) → 422 ; APPLIED/DUPLICATE → 200 ; PENDING → 202\nexcept StoreError, Contention: → 503\nexcept Exception: log with traceback → 500\n```\n\n**Status code policy.** Any 2xx means the effect is durable.\n\n| Situation | Status | `body.status` |\n|---|---|---|\n| Missing, duplicated or malformed signature header; malformed JSON or `id` | 400 | `bad_request` |\n| Bad signature, or `t` more than 300 s off | 401 | `unauthorized` (no detail in the response) |\n| Same `id`, different body | 409 | `conflict` |\n| Known type that breaks a rule or fails validation | 422 | `rejected` + `reason` |\n| Applied / duplicate / unknown type | 200 | `applied` / `duplicate` / `ignored` |\n| Refund parked | 202 | `pending` |\n| `StoreError`, compare-and-set contention | 503 | `retry` |\n| Bug | 500 | `error` |\n\n**Failure and recovery.** Every store write is either idempotent (event record, anomaly) or conditional (account compare-and-set). Every `StoreError` returns 503, and PayCo retries. A write that raised but actually committed is caught on redelivery by `applied_event_ids`. Reads (`balance`, `entries`) let `StoreError` propagate, because returning 0 would be a wrong answer. Scaling: a compare-and-set per account means contention only on one hot account, which is negligible at this volume.\n\n## 8. Data Design\n\n| Key | Contents | Written by | Write rule |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `event:{id}` | `body_sha256`, `type`, `raw_body`, `first_seen_at` | repository (via service) | put-if-absent; never updated |\n| `account:{account_id}` | see below | repository (via rules) | compare-and-set on `version`; **the only write that moves money** |\n| `anomaly:{event_id}` | reason, `raw_body`, `seen_at`, count | repository | overwrite with the same content (idempotent) |\n\n```\naccount:{id} = {\n  version, currency | null, balance,\n  entries: [{seq, event_id, type, amount(signed), currency, payment_id, created, applied_at}],\n  applied_event_ids: {...},                       # dedup lives with the money\n  payments: {payment_id: {event_id, amount, currency, refunded_by | null, source}},\n  pending_refunds: {payment_id: {event_id, amount, currency, created, received_at, mismatch}}\n}\n```\n\n- **System of record:** the account document for balances and entries; `event:*` for \"what PayCo sent us\".\n- **Consistency:** the invariants `balance == sum(entries.amount)`, at most one refund per payment, and one currency per account all hold because they change in one atomic write. `payments` and `pending_refunds` exist from M1, so adding refunds in M2 needs no data migration.\n- **Access patterns:** point lookups only; no scans on the hot path. The parked-refund alert and the reconciliation tool need to list `account:*`. If the store can't list keys, keep an `accounts_index` document (T1 decides).\n- **Retention and backup:** keep everything (A9). The managed DB's backups give the restore point. **After a restore**, events that were acknowledged after the backup are gone, and PayCo won't resend them. Recovery is to run `tools/reconcile.py` against PayCo's export and replay the missing events. Write this into the runbook in M3.\n- **Classification:** account IDs, amounts, currency. No card data. The secret is never stored or logged. Logs carry event IDs and outcomes, not bodies.\n- **Schema changes:** the account document carries `schema: 1`. Readers accept N and N−1, and documents are upgraded when next written. Revisit splitting entries into separate records if any account passes about 10k entries or 1 MB.\n\n## 9. Key Flows\n\n**F1: Payment, normal path.** Signature OK → event record created → account compare-and-set adds +2500 and fixes the currency to EUR → 200 `applied`.\n\n**F2: Partial write, then redelivery (failure path).**\n1. Event record written. Account compare-and-set raises `StoreError` → 503. Two cases: (a) it didn't commit; (b) it committed, but the client raised anyway.\n2. PayCo retries with a fresh `t` (A2). The event record already exists with the same digest, so we continue.\n3. Case (a): compare-and-set applies → 200. Case (b): `applied_event_ids` contains the ID → 200 `duplicate`. The balance is right either way.\n\nContrast: if we had written a \"processed\" flag first, case (a) would leave the event marked done and the money never applied.\n\n**F3: Refund before payment, including a race.**\n1. Refund `evt_R` for `pay_9` arrives; the account has no `pay_9` → parked → 202.\n2. Payment `evt_P` arrives. In the same compare-and-set it applies +2500, finds `pending_refunds[pay_9]`, checks amount and currency, and applies −2500. Entries read: payment, then refund.\n3. If both arrive at once, both compare-and-set on `account:acct_42`. One loses and retries against the new state, so neither can miss the other.\n\n**F4: Same `id`, different body.** Signature is valid; the event record exists with a different digest → 409, log `INCIDENT`, page someone. The account isn't read or written. Every later delivery of that body gets 409 again.\n\n## 10. Key Decisions\n\n| Decision | Options considered | Rationale | Reversibility | Revisit if |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **D1** Commit point = compare-and-set on one per-account document | (a) one atomic write per account; (b) separate records written as idempotent steps, with the balance derived from them; (c) a multi-key DB transaction | (a) needs only one conditional write, which is the weakest store capability that gives atomicity, and serialises out-of-order pairs for free (drivers 1 and 3). (b) needs per-account listing and still has races in pairing. (c) is best if it exists, but isn't known to | Hard (data model) | T1 shows transactions → use (c) inside the repository; same rules. No conditional write → **D1b:** one writer process with per-account `threading.Lock`, documented as a deployment constraint |\n| **D2** Duplicate = event ID inside the account document; different-body check = write-once `event:{id}` storing the raw-bytes SHA-256 | Raw bytes vs canonical JSON hash; a \"seen\" flag vs \"applied\" | \"Applied\" sits next to the money, so nothing is lost on a crash. Raw bytes match the brief's \"same body\" guarantee. A false positive costs an alert, not money | Medium | 409s where the canonical JSON matches → switch to the canonical hash |\n| **D3** Park early refunds (202) | Park; reject and rely on retries; apply straight away as a negative entry | Parking survives a payment arriving more than 72 h later. It keeps \"every refund matches an earlier payment\" true. It handles a new account with no currency yet | Medium | Parking is rare and the alert never fires → keep. Partial refunds introduced → rework (§17) |\n| **D4** Synchronous processing in the request | Synchronous; acknowledge to a queue and process later | An acknowledge-then-process design returns 2xx before the effect is durable, unless we add a durable queue. PayCo's retries already are one | Easy | p99 nears PayCo's timeout (Q3) |\n| **D5** Unknown types → 200 and store the raw body | 200 and store; 4xx so PayCo keeps them | Avoids 72 h of retry noise; we can backfill disputes later from `event:*` | Easy | — |\n| **D6** Rule violations → 422 plus an anomaly record | 422; 2xx and quarantine | Stays visible in PayCo's dashboard, and a code fix shipped within 72 h is picked up by retries. The anomaly record covers longer | Easy | Q4 answer |\n| **D7** Balance stored in the document, not summed on each read | Stored; computed | O(1) read; written in the same atomic write, so it can't drift; the audit asserts it equals the sum | Easy | — |\n\n## 11. Cross-Cutting Concerns\n\n- **Security (M1):**\n  - Forged webhooks → HMAC with constant-time compare.\n  - Replay → ±300 s plus idempotency.\n  - Event-ID reuse → 409 plus a page.\n  - Ambiguous JSON → duplicate keys rejected.\n  - Timing and format attacks → format checked before compare.\n  - Large-body DoS → the HTTP adapter caps bodies at 256 KB before calling `handle` (M3).\n  - The secret comes from the platform secret manager and is never logged.\n  - `balance` and `entries` have no authentication, so they must be reachable only from inside the network.\n  - Rotation: the constructor takes one secret. Rotating means an overlap window with PayCo, or a later API change (§17).\n- **Reliability (M1–M3):** RPO = 0 for acknowledged events, since we acknowledge only after commit. Outages shorter than 72 h lose nothing, because PayCo retries. Freshness target in A-table. The compare-and-set retry is bounded (5 attempts). No retry inside a request on `StoreError` in M1; add one if A2 fails.\n- **Observability:** one structured JSON log line per delivery (`event_id`, `type`, `outcome`, `status`, `ms`), built in M1. Metrics and alerts come in M3 with the platform:\n\n  | Alert | Response |\n  |---|---|\n  | Any 409 | Page |\n  | More than 5 signature or timestamp rejections in 10 min | Secret or clock problem; ticket |\n  | 5xx above 2% for 15 min | Page |\n  | Refund parked longer than 24 h | Ticket |\n  | New anomaly | Ticket |\n  | No deliveries for 6 h during business hours | Ticket |\n  | Reconciliation difference ≠ 0 | Ticket to Finance and engineering |\n\n- **Performance:** under 1 req/s today. The only bottleneck is store round-trips: 2–3 per event. A smoke load test at 10 req/s runs in M3.\n- **Cost:** one small process plus existing DB storage (about 0.4 GB/year). Negligible.\n- **Operations:** the owning team runs it with business-hours support, and pages only for 409 and sustained 5xx. Runbooks (M3) cover: 409 incident; parked refund ageing; anomaly triage and replay; restore followed by reconcile-and-replay.\n- **AI-specific:** not applicable; there are no model components.\n\n## 12. Build Sequence\n\nTeam assumption: one Python engineer full time, a reviewer about 10% of the time, a Finance contact a few hours a week. It says the directory is intentionally empty and does **not** document `ledgerkit` or `MemoryStore`, even though the brief points there. I couldn't see which operations the store supports. That matters more than anything else in this plan, because how we survive `StoreError` partway through a request depends on whether the store has conditional writes or transactions. Below I design against a small set of store operations I'm assuming exist (§5, A1). I also give the fallback if they don't. Checking this is the first task (T1).\n\n---\n\n## 1. Summary\n\n- **What:** Ledger is a stdlib-only Python library, `LedgerService`. It turns signed PayCo webhooks into per-account balances and entry lists that Finance can reconcile against PayCo's monthly statement, to the minor unit. It replaces the nightly CSV-to-spreadsheet script and the manual balance fixes.\n- **Shape:** One synchronous library called by a thin HTTP adapter. Internally it has a functional core and a thin I/O layer: pure modules for signature checking, parsing and balance rules, plus one repository module that talks to the store. There is no queue and no second service. PayCo's 72-hour retries act as our retry queue.\n- **Key decisions:**\n  1. **One atomic write moves money.** Each account's state (balance, entries, payment index, parked refunds, IDs of applied events) lives in one account document. It changes only through a single compare-and-set write, which is the commit point. A `StoreError` at any point leaves either \"nothing happened\" or \"everything happened\", and PayCo's redelivery finishes the job.\n  2. **Return 2xx only after the effect is durable.** A duplicate is recognised from the account document (the event was applied), not from a separate \"seen\" flag. A crash between \"seen\" and \"applied\" therefore can't lose money.\n  3. **Write-once event record** keyed by event `id`, holding the SHA-256 of the raw body. If the same `id` arrives with a different body, we return 409, raise an alert, and leave the account untouched. The record also covers unknown event types and stores their raw body, so we can replay them once we support disputes and payouts.\n  4. **A refund that arrives before its payment is parked** (202) inside the account document. It is settled in the same atomic write that later applies the payment. We don't reject it and hope PayCo's retries outlast the gap.\n  5. **Strict input handling:** we verify the HMAC over the raw bytes before parsing, allow ±300 s on the timestamp, compare in constant time, and parse JSON strictly (duplicate keys, floats, booleans and NaN are rejected as amounts).\n- **First milestone:** two short spikes (store semantics, and how PayCo signs retries) and the payment path end to end. It includes signature checks, deduplication, the different-body check, unknown types, and a test that injects a fault at every write and shows redelivery always ends in the same state as a fault-free run.\n- **Top risks:** the store has no conditional write (A1); PayCo retries reuse the original `t`, so retries more than 5 minutes later fail the timestamp check (A2); refunds of payments made before cutover arrive with no matching payment (§15).\n\n## 2. Context and Goals\n\n- **Problem:** Balances are rebuilt nightly from a CSV and fixed by hand. They are up to 24 hours stale, errors are possible, and support staff spend time on it.\n- **Goals:**\n  - Every validly signed PayCo payment and refund ends up applied **exactly once**, or is visibly parked or rejected. Nothing is silently lost or doubled.\n  - A balance reflects a payment within about 60 s of PayCo sending it, in normal operation (assumption).\n  - Survive `StoreError`, duplicate delivery, out-of-order delivery and concurrent delivery without manual repair.\n- **Non-goals:** debiting customer spend (not in the interface; see Q2), partial refunds, disputes, payouts and other event types (recorded but not applied), multi-currency accounts, the HTTP server, deployment and monitoring stack (covered here as guidance only), and secret rotation with two secrets live at once (deferred, §17).\n- **Success measures:** zero unexplained differences in the first two monthly reconciliations after cutover; zero manual balance edits; nightly script retired; no 409 that isn't explained.\n\n## 3. Drivers, Requirements, and Constraints\n\n**Ranked quality attributes**\n\n| # | Attribute | Measurable target | Why it matters |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1 | Financial correctness | 0 unexplained differences per account per monthly reconciliation. In a seeded simulation of 10k events with shuffled order, duplicates and injected faults, final state equals the oracle (an independent calculation of the expected result) | Finance needs an exact match; a wrong balance is real money |\n| 2 | Authenticity and integrity | 0 money movements from unsigned, stale (>300 s) or different-body deliveries; every different-body case alerts within 5 min | Webhook endpoints are public; the brief makes different-body reuse an incident |\n| 3 | Recovery from partial failure | For every write position *k* in a request, with a `StoreError` before or after it commits, redelivery ends in the same state as a fault-free run | The store fails partway through requests |\n| 4 | Evolvability | Adding a new event type (e.g. `charge.dispute.*`) in ≤1 week with no change to stored data shape, plus replay of events already received | PayCo adds types; \"we will add them later\" |\n| 5 | Operability and simplicity | One deployable unit; ≤5 alert types; on-call needs no store access for routine cases *(assumption)* | Small team, small volume |\n| — | Latency and throughput | p99 handling < 1 s at 10 req/s *(assumption; about 100× today's volume)* | Not a driver at a few thousand events a day. Recorded so nobody over-builds |\n\n**Key functional requirements:** verify the signature and timestamp; credit `payment.succeeded`; debit `refund.succeeded` once per payment, with the amount equal to the payment; the account currency is fixed by its first payment; a different body under the same `id` is rejected; unknown types are accepted and not applied; `balance` and `entries` match the interface in the brief.\n\n**Constraints:** Python, standard library only; the store is a `ledgerkit` MemoryStore client (API unknown to me); the interface signatures are fixed; HTTP, deployment and monitoring live outside this codebase.\n\n**Hard parts**\n\n1. **Atomicity against a store that fails partway through.** If we mark an event \"processed\" before the money moves, a crash loses money for good, because the redelivery looks like a duplicate.\n2. **Out-of-order and concurrent pairs.** A refund that arrives before its payment, or both arriving at the same moment, can leave a refund parked forever unless both are serialised on one record.\n3. **Cutover.** Refunds of payments made before go-live, and opening balances. Easy to miss, and expensive if missed.\n4. **PayCo delivery details we haven't verified:** whether retries get a fresh `t`, and whether redelivered bodies are byte-identical.\n\n## 4. Current State\n\n- **Code:** none. `README.md` is the only file and says so. `ledgerkit` is not in the workspace, so its API, version and the exact behaviour of `StoreError` are unknown.\n- **Process:** a nightly script copies PayCo's CSV export into a spreadsheet, and support staff fix balances by hand. This is the system Ledger replaces, and the source of opening balances (§15).\n- **Conventions I'll set, since none exist:** package `ledger/`, tests in `tests/` run with `python -m unittest`, no third-party packages apart from `ledgerkit`, Python ≥3.11 *(assumption A8)*.\n\n## 5. Assumptions and Open Questions\n\n**Assumptions**\n\n| # | Assumption | Impact if wrong | How and when validated |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| A1 | The store offers single-key get, put-if-absent, and compare-and-set (or a transaction). A single write is never left half-applied. | Without a conditional write: fall back to one writer process with per-account locks (D1b). With half-applied writes: no client-side design is safe, so escalate to the DB owner. | T1 spike, day 1 |\n| A2 | Each PayCo retry is signed again with a fresh `t`. | Retries more than 300 s later always fail, so our 503s never recover. We'd need to retry inside the request and escalate to PayCo. | T2 sandbox spike, M1 |\n| A3 | Redeliveries are byte-identical (the brief says \"same body\"). | False 409s on events already applied. No money effect, but alert noise. | T2; incident logs also record whether canonical JSON matched |\n| A4 | At most one `refund.succeeded` per `payment_id` (refunds are always full).
